Field surveys conducted along the continental shelf of Namibia have provided detailed life-history data for Benguela hake (Merluccius polli). Juveniles initially inhabit shallower waters before migrating to deeper grounds as they mature. Tagging studies indicate that females reach a total length at puberty of 40 cm [Lp = 40 cm], a size typically attained by the fourth or fifth year of life. This length at maturity is consistent with values reported for other Merluccius species inhabiting similar upwelling ecosystems. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of mature individuals reaches a maximum value of 25% [GSI = 25%] under the cool, productive conditions characteristic of the Benguela Current at 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. Histological examination of ovarian tissue confirms that vitellogenesis is initiated when females reach approximately 37 to 44 cm in length, corroborating the estimated size at first maturity. Female hake exhibit a group-synchronous oocyte development pattern, with a single annual spawning pulse coinciding with the peak of the upwelling season.

The neonatal mass of Benguela hake is remarkably small, reflecting the pelagic spawning strategy and the energy constraints imposed upon a yolk-sac larva prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. Fertilised ova measure approximately 0.9 mm in diameter, and the resulting wet weight at birth is calculated to be roughly 0.00038 g [Wwb = roughly 0.00038 g]. This minimal initial mass is typical of gadiform fishes that produce large numbers of small, planktonic larvae. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on its endogenous reserves until mouth opening and retinal differentiation permit the first exogenous feeding. The duration of this lecithotrophic phase is temperature-dependent, and under the thermal regime of the northern Benguela system, the trophic switch occurs within a few days. The small size of the newly emerged larvae makes them highly vulnerable to predation and starvation, and mortality rates during the early larval stages are correspondingly high, representing a critical bottleneck for recruitment.

Estimates of asymptotic size for Merluccius polli are derived from large-scale commercial catch data and scientific survey trawls. Commercial trawl surveys consistently document an ultimate total length of 80 cm [Li = 80 cm] for this species, a value that represents the maximum size observed among older, slow-growing individuals. This asymptotic length is somewhat lower than that reported for the co-occurring deep-water hake (Merluccius paradoxus), suggesting a degree of niche partitioning in the vertical dimension of the water column. Based on the length-weight relationship observed for the population, individuals attaining this length reach an ultimate wet weight of 3600 g [Wwi = 3600 g]. Individuals approaching this asymptotic size exhibit substantially reduced somatic growth rates, with increments of less than a few centimetres per year in the oldest age classes. These large, reproductively mature adults constitute the spawning stock biomass that drives the annual reproductive output of the population along the Angolan and Namibian coasts.

Reproductive investment in female Benguela hake is closely tied to body size, with larger, older females contributing disproportionately to the total egg production of the stock. The wet weight at puberty, marking the body mass at which females first become capable of participating in the annual spawning event, has been estimated at 425 g [Wwp = 425 g], a value consistent with those reported for other Merluccius species inhabiting productive upwelling zones. This mass corresponds closely to the 40 cm length threshold established for the onset of sexual maturation. Field studies indicate that first-time spawners tend to produce fewer, smaller eggs than their more experienced counterparts, a pattern that has been documented for several other batch-spawning teleosts. The energetic cost of the first reproductive effort, coupled with the allocation of resources toward continued somatic growth, likely constrains early fecundity. Analysis of oocyte size-frequency distributions reveals that post-pubertal females undergo at least one full cycle of gonadal recrudescence annually, with the peak of spawning activity observed during the austral winter months.

The maximum lifespan of Benguela hake in the wild, under the prevailing environmental conditions of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], has been estimated at approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years], based on otolith increment counts from specimens collected across the species' geographic range. This longevity is comparable to that observed in other slow-growing, late-maturing gadids from temperate and subtropical upwelling zones. Individuals in the oldest age classes, those approaching 7,300 days, show clear signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced fecundity and a higher incidence of atretic oocytes. Natural mortality rates increase markedly beyond the fifteenth year, reflecting the gradual decline in physiological condition associated with senescence. The combination of a 20-year maximum lifespan, a relatively late age at maturity, and a low natural mortality rate among adults positions Merluccius polli as a relatively k-selected species within the context of the Benguela Current ecosystem, making the population particularly sensitive to sustained overfishing.
